Induction therapy with antilymphocyte immunoglobulins or muromonab-CD3 has declined due to the high inci- dence of infection and lymphoproliferative disease associ- ated with their use, and they are generally reserved for the treatment of corticosteroid-resistant acute rejection.2,4,8,9 The use of interleukin-2 receptor antibodies, basiliximab, and daclizumab, is increasing;10 initial studies suggest they decrease the number of rejection episodes.8,9 It has been suggested that they may be of benefit in those with pre-transplant renal impairment by allowing for delayed introduction or lower doses of calcineurin inhibitors.16 The use of alemtuzumab has also been investigated.10,15 The induction of complete immune tolerance remains the ultimate goal in liver transplantation.10,17,18 It may be fea- sible to reduce or stop all immunosuppression in long-term stable liver transplant patients.6,19 The term ‘operational tolerance’ is used to define stable graft function without features of rejection and without immunosuppressive treatment; ‘prope tolerance’ refers to stable graft function in patients with minimal immunosuppression.10,19 Al- though it is not uncommon for rejection to eventually oc- cur in those withdrawn from immunosuppression, this may be reversed by resumption of therapy, with a small rate of graft loss. Favourable markers for successful withdrawal appear to be at least 2 years of post-transplant follow-up, low incidence of previous rejection episodes, non-auto-immune primary liver disease, and possibly min- imal post-transplant immunosuppression.19 Most acute rejection episodes occur during the first 3 to 6 months of therapy.12 Early acute rejection does not affect patient or graft survival6,20,21 and, if mild, may be associat- ed with increased survival.1 Late acute rejection, occurring after 30 days post-transplant may be related to reduction or withdrawal of immunosuppressive therapy.22 It has a worse prognosis, with reports of up to half of patients de- veloping graft loss.21 Corticosteroids are used in the first- line treatment of acute rejection.11,23 For corticosteroid-re- sistant rejection, muromonab-CD3 or antilymphocyte im- munoglobulins are used, and increasing the dose of tac- rolimus, or conversion from ciclosporin to tacrolimus, may also be effective.2,4,9 Interleukin-2 receptor antibodies may also be used.
